1247.title: The Athari approach
1247.hook: a man asks Imam Malik how Allah rose over the Throne, and gets an answer in four parts
1247.howItsDone: Muslims who follow the Athari approach, often associated with the Hanbali school, affirm the descriptions of Allah in the Qur'an and authentic hadith as they came, without likening Him to creation and without asking how (bila kayf).

segments.voice: Yesterday: Imam al-Maturidi of Samarqand, who gave reason a bigger job in knowing good and bad.

Medina. Imam Malik is sitting with his students when a man comes up and asks about a verse. The Qur'an says Allah rose over the Throne. How did He rise? The reports say Malik lowered his head for a long moment, and he began to sweat. Then he looked up and answered. The rising is known. The how of it is beyond grasping. Believing in it is a duty. And asking about the how is an innovation. Then, in the version people repeat, he had the man shown out.
screen: `HOW DID HE RISE?` → `MALIK LOWERS HIS HEAD.` → `THE HOW IS BEYOND GRASPING.`

segments.voice: Here's the verse, in Pickthall's translation: "The Beneficent One, Who is established on the Throne." The Athari approach takes its name from athar, a report or a trace: the narrations handed down from the Prophet Muhammad ﷺ and his companions. Its method is simple to say. When the Qur'an or an authentic hadith describes Allah, with a hand, a face, rising over the Throne, coming, laughing, affirm it as it came. Don't explain it away as a figure of speech. Don't picture it like a human body. And don't ask how: in Arabic, bila kayf, without how. A saying reported from several early scholars puts it in one line: pass these texts on as they came. Ahmad ibn Hanbal, who stood through the trial, is remembered as holding this way, and the approach has been tied with the Hanbali school since; later, Ibn Taymiyya defended it at length. Notice the difference from the last few days. The Mu'tazilah reasoned their way to a created Qur'an. Al-Ash'ari and al-Maturidi built careful arguments to defend tradition. The Atharis were often wary of kalam itself, not because they disliked thinking, but because they believed some questions about Allah are not ours to answer, and that the words He chose are enough. There's a discipline in that: letting a verse about God stand, without filling the gap with pictures. Ash'aris and Maturidis also used this restraint at times. The schools argue about when to use it, and how far.
screen: `ATHAR: THE REPORT HANDED DOWN.` · `AFFIRM, DON'T PICTURE.` · `BILA KAYF: WITHOUT HOW.` · then, large: `PASS IT ON AS IT CAME.`

segments.voice: Say the verse slowly, aloud or in your head: The Beneficent One, Who is established on the Throne. Each time your mind reaches for a picture, a chair, a sky, a king, set it down gently, the way Malik set down the question, and keep only the words. If you'd rather, rest on the two words without how.
The Athari approach. The way of the early reports: affirm what Allah says of Himself, as it came, without likening and without asking how. Today's word.
Your line: as it came. The words are let stand, without a picture. Rest well.

1248.title: Shia theology
1248.hook: roots and branches: how Twelver Shia teaching sets out the beliefs that hold everything up
1248.howItsDone: Twelver Shia Muslims learn the usul al-din, the roots of religion (tawhid, 'adl, nubuwwa, imama and ma'ad), and are taught to hold them through their own understanding, while following a qualified scholar in matters of practice.

segments.voice: Yesterday: the Athari approach, which affirms what Allah says of Himself as it came, without asking how.

A tree has branches you can see: leaves, fruit, the shade you sit in. And it has roots you can't see, holding the whole thing up. Twelver Shia teaching uses exactly that picture. Prayer, fasting, pilgrimage, charity: those are furu' al-din, the branches of religion. The beliefs underneath are usul al-din, the roots. And one detail stands out. In the branches, Twelver Shia Muslims follow a qualified scholar's rulings. In the roots, the teaching goes, each person should hold the beliefs through their own understanding, not just because someone said so.
screen: `BRANCHES YOU CAN SEE.` → `ROOTS YOU CAN'T.` → `HOLD THE ROOTS YOURSELF.`

segments.voice: Day 865 gave you the Shia telling of who leads after the Prophet; today, the roots underneath. Twelver Shia theology names them as tawhid, the oneness of Allah; 'adl, His justice; nubuwwa, prophethood; imama, the imamate; and ma'ad, the return, the resurrection and the Last Day. Oneness, prophethood and the return appear in Sunni creeds too. Two stand out, and they're today's line. Justice first. The Qur'an says, in Pickthall's words, "Lo! Allah enjoineth justice and kindness." Shia theologians hold that Allah does nothing unjust and nothing without wisdom, and never asks of anyone what they can't do. Here Shia theology stands close to the Mu'tazilah, and the two traditions shared arguments. Then guidance. Shia teaching holds that Allah does not leave people without a guide. After the Prophet Muhammad ﷺ, guidance continues through imams from his household, beginning with Ali, divinely chosen and protected from error. In Twelver belief the twelfth imam is alive and hidden, in what's called the occultation, and will return. There's a hadith both Sunnis and Shia know. In Sahih Muslim, the Prophet says he is leaving two weighty things among his people: the Book of Allah and the people of his household. Shia scholars read it as pointing to the imams. Sunni teaching also honors the Prophet's household, but doesn't count the imamate among the roots of faith. Zaydi and Isma'ili Shia have their own accounts too. Justice and guidance: a God who is fair, and who does not leave people without a guide.

Go through them again, slower, with just the Arabic words, and stay with the root you'd most like to understand better. If you pray, you can ask for understanding in your own words.

1249.title: Free will and decree
1249.hook: two verses side by side, and the theologians who tried to hold them both
1249.howItsDone: Muslims affirm both Allah's decree and human responsibility, and the schools of theology explain how they fit in different ways, from the Ash'ari teaching of kasb to the Shia saying of 'a matter between the two'.

segments.voice: Yesterday: Twelver Shia theology, its roots of belief, and justice and guidance at its heart.

The caliph Umar is on the road to Syria when word comes: plague has broken out in the land ahead. He hears his advisers disagree, and decides to turn back. Abu Ubayda, a companion of the Prophet, objects. Are you running from the decree of Allah? Umar's answer is in Sahih al-Bukhari: yes, we run from the decree of Allah to the decree of Allah. If your camels came down into a valley with one green side and one bare one, wouldn't you graze them by Allah's decree whichever side you chose? The theologians made this a hard question. If Allah decrees everything, what's left for my choice? And if my choice is real, what's left for His decree?
screen: `PLAGUE AHEAD.` → `FROM DECREE TO DECREE.` → `WHAT'S LEFT FOR ME?`

segments.voice: Start with two verses, in Pickthall's translation. One says: "Then whosoever will, let him believe, and whosoever will, let him disbelieve." A real choice, handed to us. Another says: "Yet ye will not, unless Allah willeth." Every choice resting inside His will. The Qur'an puts both on the page and doesn't apologize for either, and the theologians of this part each tried to hold them together. The Mu'tazilah leaned on the first: a just God only judges people for acts truly their own, so humans bring their acts into being. The Ash'aris leaned on another verse: "When Allah hath created you and what ye make?" Allah creates every act, they said, and the human being acquires it, takes it on, and is answerable for it. Their word is kasb, acquisition. The Maturidis said Allah creates the act, the human being's free choice is real, and it's that choice that is judged. And Shia theology has a saying it traces to Imam Ja'far al-Sadiq: neither compulsion nor complete handing over, but a matter between the two. None of them says we're puppets, and none says Allah steps aside. Each is trying to keep both verses true at once. And Umar's answer at the edge of the plague is one anyone can use: even choosing the green side of the valley sits inside the decree. Do your part with your whole effort, then let the outcome rest with Allah.

Then picture the moment after, and let go of how it lands; that part isn't yours to hold. If you pray, you can hand the outcome to Allah in your own words.

1250.title: Why suffering?
1250.hook: the Qur'an promises tests, and tells a story about a wisdom that only shows up later
1250.howItsDone: Muslims meet hardship with patience, sabr, and say "we are Allah's and unto Him we are returning" at news of a death or loss; grief and tears are not forbidden, and the Prophet himself wept.

segments.voice: Yesterday: free will and decree, and Umar's road: do your part, then trust Allah with the rest.

"And surely We shall try you with something of fear and hunger, and loss of wealth and lives and crops; but give glad tidings to the steadfast." That's the Qur'an, in Pickthall's translation. It doesn't promise an easy life; it promises tests. The next verse describes the steadfast: when misfortune strikes them, they say, "Lo! we are Allah's and lo! unto Him we are returning." Muslims say it at news of a death or a loss. The theologians argued long about why a just and merciful God allows pain.
screen: `WE SHALL TRY YOU.` → `FEAR, HUNGER, LOSS.` → `UNTO HIM WE ARE RETURNING.`

segments.voice: You met the Qur'an's clearest picture on day 468: Musa and al-Khidr, in Surah al-Kahf. Musa travels with a servant of Allah given knowledge from Him; tradition calls him al-Khidr. Musa asks to learn from him, and is warned he won't be able to bear it. Then three strange things happen. Al-Khidr makes a hole in the boat of poor people who gave them a ride. He kills a boy. And in a town that refused them food, he rebuilds a falling wall and asks nothing for it. Each time Musa protests, and each time he's reminded of the warning. At the parting, al-Khidr explains. A king was seizing every boat by force; a damaged one might be passed over. The boy would have burdened his believing parents with rebellion and disbelief. The wall hid treasure belonging to two orphans, and it had to stand until they were grown. What Musa saw as harm had a purpose he couldn't see. And another verse: "Allah knoweth, ye know not." That doesn't make pain small, and Islam doesn't ask anyone to pretend it is. When the Prophet Muhammad's ﷺ son Ibrahim was dying, Sahih al-Bukhari records that his eyes filled with tears. He said the eye weeps and the heart grieves, and we say only what pleases our Lord. A hadith in Sahih Muslim says the believer's affair is all good: thankful in ease, patient in hardship, and both bring good. It doesn't say every loss makes sense today. The story of the boat says the wisdom is not always seen.

segments.voice: Let one hard thing come to mind, not the hardest, one you can hold for two minutes, and don't hurry to explain it; if grief comes, let it come, the Prophet wept. Then set one more thought beside the question, without pushing it away: I may not see all of it. If you pray, say, unto Him we are returning; and if a loss feels too heavy to carry alone, in the US call or text 988, any hour, or elsewhere, local emergency help.

Your line: not always seen. Tears and trust, side by side, in the same breath. Rest well.

1251.title: The attributes
1251.hook: one verse says nothing is like Him, and in the same breath calls Him the Hearer, the Seer
1251.howItsDone: Muslims call on Allah by His names and attributes, such as as-Sami', the Hearer, and al-Basir, the Seer, while holding with Qur'an 42:11 that nothing is like Him; the schools of theology explain the attributes in different ways.

segments.voice: Yesterday: why suffering, and a wisdom not always seen, with tears and trust side by side.

One sentence of the Qur'an, in two halves. The first half, in Pickthall's translation: "Naught is as His likeness." Nothing is like Him. Then, in the same breath: "and He is the Hearer, the Seer." Hearing and seeing are things you do. A child does them. A cat does them. So the verse that says nothing is like Allah goes straight on to describe Him with words we use for ourselves. That isn't a slip. It's the whole problem of this part in one line.
screen: `NAUGHT IS AS HIS LIKENESS.` → `AND HE IS THE HEARER, THE SEER.` → `BOTH IN ONE VERSE.`

segments.voice: Day 232 gave you the most beautiful names; today, how theologians speak of them. The Arabic word is sifat, attributes: the qualities Allah describes Himself with, knowing, willing, powerful, living, hearing, seeing, speaking. Another verse says: "Allah's are the fairest names. Invoke Him by them." So Muslims call on Him by what He has said of Himself. But how do you use those words without shrinking Him to our size? Theologians name two ditches beside the road. One is tashbih, likening: hearing like ours, only bigger, with ears and a place to stand. The other is ta'til, emptying out: deciding the words mean nothing at all. The road runs between, and each school we've met walks it its own way. The Atharis affirm hearing and seeing as they came, and don't ask how. The Ash'aris and Maturidis affirm a set of attributes as real and eternal, set out by argument, and explain some other descriptions with care. The Mu'tazilah, guarding oneness, said Allah knows and hears by His very essence, not by attributes added to Him. And Shia theology has its own careful version of that concern. Different routes, one shared fence: He is not like His creation. As theologians put it, He hears, but not with ears. He sees, but not with eyes. The word hearing is true of Him; the picture that comes with it isn't.

segments.voice: Listen, and loosely count the sounds you can hear, a fan, traffic, your own breath, and notice how few you can hold at once: that's our hearing, limited and needing ears. Now hold the word the verse uses, the Hearer, without building a picture: hearing without any of those limits, and without our shape. If you pray, you can call on Him by that name, as-Sami'; if you don't, let the phrase nothing like Him be enough.
Sifat. The attributes of Allah: hearing, seeing, knowing, willing and more, affirmed without likening Him to anything. Today's word.
Your line: nothing like him. Real names, and no picture big enough to hold them. Go gently.

1252.title: The miracle of the Qur'an
1252.hook: a challenge sits inside the book itself: bring one surah like it
1252.howItsDone: Muslims speak of the Qur'an as the Prophet's lasting miracle, and scholars of Arabic rhetoric and theology have written works on i'jaz, studying what in its language and arrangement they hold cannot be matched.

segments.voice: Yesterday: sifat, the attributes, real names for One who is nothing like us.

A book usually asks to be believed. This one sets a test. In the second surah, al-Baqarah, the Qur'an turns to anyone who doubts where it came from and says, in Pickthall's translation: "then produce a surah of the like thereof, and call your witness beside Allah if ye are truthful." Not the whole book. One surah. The challenge is printed in the middle of the text it's defending, and it is read aloud whenever that surah is recited.
screen: `A BOOK THAT SETS A TEST.` → `PRODUCE A SURAH LIKE IT.` → `THE CHALLENGE IS ON THE PAGE.`

segments.voice: The word is i'jaz. Lane's old Arabic lexicon puts it under a root about being unable, falling short. A mu'jizah, a miracle, is a sign that leaves others unable to match it. Musa had his staff. 'Isa, in the Qur'an, healed the blind. So what was the sign given to the Prophet Muhammad, peace be upon him? A hadith in Sahih al-Bukhari gives his own answer, in paraphrase: every prophet was given signs that led people to believe, and what I was given is revelation that Allah revealed to me. The miracle, Muslims say, is the book. Another verse widens the challenge, Pickthall again: "though mankind and the jinn should assemble to produce the like of this Qur'an, they could not produce the like thereof though they were helpers one of another." Then the theologians got to work, and they did not all agree on what exactly can't be matched. Al-Baqillani, who wrote a whole book on i'jaz, pointed to its eloquence, which he held was beyond the reach of Arabic poetry. Al-Jurjani pointed to its nazm, the way its words are joined and arranged. Some pointed to what it tells of things unseen. And one Mu'tazili thinker, al-Nazzam, is remembered for a different answer: people could have matched it, but Allah turned them away from trying. Other scholars rejected that view, but it shows how seriously the question was taken. So this part ends where it began, with kalam: faith asking questions of its own book. A staff or a healing is seen once. A book can be opened again tomorrow.

1253.title: Death and return
1253.hook: the soul is drawn out and returns to its Lord
1253.howItsDone: When a Muslim is dying, family often sit close and gently remind them of the shahada, la ilaha illa Allah, and on hearing of a death Muslims say inna lillahi wa inna ilayhi raji'un, we belong to Allah and to Him we return.

segments.voice: Yesterday: i'jaz, the Qur'an as a sign no one can match, and the end of the theologians' part.

A hospital room, late. The machines hum. Around the bed, a family speaks softly, and someone leans close to the person lying there and says, gently, la ilaha illa Allah. There is no god but God. They aren't asking for anything. They are reminding. A hadith in Sahih Muslim tells Muslims to do exactly this: prompt your dying to say la ilaha illa Allah. So the last words hoped for at that bed are the first words of the faith.
screen: `A ROOM, LATE, A FAMILY.` → `LA ILAHA ILLA ALLAH, SOFTLY.` → `THE FIRST WORDS, AT THE LAST.`

segments.voice: Day 686 called death a return; today, the moment itself. The word is mawt, death, and the Qur'an slows down for it. In Surah al-Waqi'ah, it describes the soul rising to the throat while the people around the bed look on, and adds, in paraphrase: and We are nearer to him than you, though you do not see. The family is close. Allah, the verse says, is closer. Then a long hadith, narrated by al-Bara' ibn 'Azib and collected by Imam Ahmad, with a shorter version in Abu Dawud, tells it as a scene. Angels come to the dying. For the believer, they come with bright faces, and the soul is drawn out gently, the hadith says, the way a drop flows from the mouth of a water skin. For the one who turned away, it is described as hard, like a skewer pulled through wet wool. The scene is read as both comfort and warning. And then the direction. Death in the Qur'an is not a disappearing; it is a going back. In Surah al-Fajr the soul at rest is addressed, and Pickthall gives it like this: "But ah! thou soul at peace! Return unto thy Lord, content in His good pleasure!" The soul came from somewhere, and it is called home. That's why a hadith in Tirmidhi tells Muslims to remember death often, calling it the destroyer of pleasures. Not to be gloomy, but to keep the pleasures in their place. Someone who remembers they are going back tends to pack more carefully.
screen: `NEARER THAN THOSE AROUND THE BED.` · `DRAWN OUT LIKE A DROP FROM A WATER SKIN.` · `THOU SOUL AT PEACE, RETURN.` · then, large: `REMEMBER IT, AND PACK CAREFULLY.`

segments.voice: If this is too heavy today, stop here and simply breathe; that's allowed. Otherwise, notice the breath going out and the small pause before it comes back, hold lightly the thought that one day it won't, and ask: if I were called back today, what would I want to have done this week? If you pray, say quietly, la ilaha illa Allah, or rest on the word return; and if dark thoughts come and stay, in the US call or text 988, any hour, or elsewhere, local emergency help.
Mawt. Death: in Muslim teaching, the soul drawn out and returning to its Lord. Today's word.
Your line: return. A new part begins here: the unseen journey. That's today, done.
